analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to cover autism and developmental disorder treatment for children under 22.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required group health plans covering medical and surgical benefits to also cover treatment for autism and related developmental disorders — therapy, respite care, and rehabilitative care for anyone under 22. It barred insurers from putting special dollar caps or higher cost-sharing on that coverage, and from dropping families just to dodge the rule. It exempted small employers (50 or fewer workers) and any plan whose costs would rise by 1% or more. It was referred to two House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under 22 who have autism or other developmental disorders and are covered by employer health plans. Their therapy, respite, and rehabilitative care would have been covered on the same terms as other medical care, with no special dollar caps and no higher deductibles or coinsurance than other benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans that cover medical and surgical benefits would have to cover pervasive developmental disorders, including therapeutic, respite, and rehabilitative care for anyone under 22 [S2][S3].

Plans could not impose annual or lifetime dollar limits on that coverage unless the same limits applied to all medical and surgical benefits, and could not charge higher deductibles or coinsurance for it than for other care [S2][S3].
Plans and insurers could not deny eligibility or renewal solely to avoid the new requirements, and the rules applied separately to in-network and out-of-network benefits [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and the health insurers who administer their plans would bear the added cost of covering behavioral therapy, respite, and rehabilitative care, which is often expensive and was frequently excluded. That cost would partly show up in premiums paid by employers and workers.

drawbacks.text: The bill contained a broad escape hatch: it did not apply to any plan whose costs would rise by 1% or more, so an insurer could avoid the mandate entirely by showing a modest cost increase [S3].
It exempted all employers with 50 or fewer workers, leaving employees of small businesses — a large share of the workforce — without the new coverage [S2][S3].
Mandated coverage raises premiums, and some of that cost falls on workers and employers who never use the benefit, including employees without children affected by autism.
The definition of 'pervasive developmental disorder' incorporated the federal definition of 'developmental disability,' a broad category, so the mandate went beyond autism alone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families facing autism treatment bills that can run into tens of thousands of dollars a year, guaranteed coverage with no special caps or higher cost-sharing is a large, concrete benefit. The main costs are higher premiums spread across plan participants, and the bill's own exemptions — the 1% cost increase carve-out and the small-employer exemption — would have limited both the benefit and the cost in practice. The narrow escape clause makes the mandate much weaker than it first appears, but it also blunts the objection that costs would balloon.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee for the rest of the Congress: it was referred to two House committees, then to a subcommittee, and no markup, hearing vote, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Wexler introduced the bill on January 16, 2008, and it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
On February 28, 2008, part of it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was taken [S5].
The bill drew 7 cosponsors, all Democrats, and none of the committees ever voted on it before the 110th Congress ended [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and large employers avoided the new coverage mandate and its cost, while families with autistic children got no relief.

for.name: Robert Wexler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to two committees

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support was one Democratic sponsor and 7 Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican cosponsors listed [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers to cover autism and developmental disorder therapy on parity terms, a category of care plans often limited or excluded. Insurers bore the direct cost, though the 1% cost-increase exemption gave them a way out.
Employers sponsoring group plans would have faced higher premium and benefits costs to fund the new coverage; small employers were exempt.

industries.industry: Behavioral therapy and autism treatment providers
industries.note: A coverage mandate would have created insured demand for therapy, respite, and rehabilitative services, expanding access for patients and revenue for providers.
